tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the repo carries the full raw data behind the README table (benches/results/blacksmith-2026-10-09-37989957431 and -37999607702: measurements.json with host, rustc 1.99.0/LLVM 23.1.1, cc GCC 13.3.0 and Apple clang 21.0.0 receipts, Criterion means per case), the benchmark code is public (benches/battle_bench.rs, benches/regex_tasks.rs, benches/general_regex.rs, scripts/compare-engines.py), C Oniguruma is compiled by build.rs with cc opt_level(3) (-O3) and the Rust side with the bench profile (opt-level 3, thin LTO), and one host's CPU model is named (Apple M4 Pro, virtual). The per-host geomeans in the raw summaries reproduce the README figures (derived from page data).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (geometric means over both hosts, measured 2026-10-09): versus Oniguruma (C) 2.2x faster on 32 everyday-pattern tasks, 1.4x faster on 17 advanced-pattern tasks, 12x faster on 3 syntax-highlighting documents (C, Java, PHP scanner replays). Raw per-host summaries: everyday 2.12x on AMD EPYC and 2.39x on Apple M4 Pro, advanced 1.28x and 1.45x, highlighting documents 9.96x to 17.58x (EPYC) and 8.54x to 14.52x (M4 Pro) (derived from page data). C Oniguruma still wins some tasks on EPYC: regex_tasks rfc5322_emails 0.67, ipv6_addresses 0.64, csv_last_column_backtracking 0.89, email_validation 0.96, html_attribute_values 0.92, markdown_emphasis 0.90, password_rules 0.91, absent_comments 0.78, and C compiles several patterns 2x to 4x faster (compilation__lookbehind 0.27, ts_279_compile 0.48). Versus PCRE2 interpreter 1.7x / 1.4x / 28x faster (only tasks it can run), versus PCRE2 JIT 2.1x slower / 3.5x slower / 9.7x faster, versus Rust regex 1.5x slower on everyday patterns, versus Onigmo 2.6x / 1.5x / 34x faster.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.99.0 (LLVM 23.1.1), cargo bench --locked --features onigmo (bench profile: default opt-level 3, lto = "thin"); C Oniguruma at pinned commit f95747b462de672b6f8dbdeb478245ddf061ca53 compiled by build.rs through the cc crate with opt_level(3) (-O3), hand-written config.h, by cc (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 on Linux and Apple clang 21.0.0 on macOS; PCRE2 linked statically (PCRE2_SYS_STATIC=1). Receipts in benches/results/blacksmith-2026-10-09-37989957431/*/measurements.json.
corrections.hardware: Blacksmith CI runners: blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-26 (Apple M4 Pro, virtual, 6 vCPUs, 24 GB, macOS 26.3) and blacksmith-4vcpu-ubuntu-2404 (AMD EPYC with AVX-512, exact model not given, 4 vCPUs, 16 GB, Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.6.141); Criterion 3 s measurement, 0.5 s warm-up, 30 samples; workflow runs 37989957431 and 37999607702 on 2026-10-09.
corrections.caveats: The speedup is not a Rust-over-C codegen win: ADR-007 and ADR-008 (docs/app/routes/adr/) document Rust-only algorithmic additions layered on the line-by-line port, among them SIMD memchr/memmem literal search, literal tries for alternations, Aho-Corasick required-literal filters, leading-class-run skips (credited with 22-31x on email-like scans, matching the 32.7x email_addresses row), leading-check jumps, Unicode range lookup changes, ASCII class runs, and for highlighting a DFA pre-filter built on the regex-automata crate plus scanner and pattern caches. Measured on shared virtual CI runners (EPYC model unnamed); author-run. C Oniguruma is built from a hand-written config.h rather than its CMake configure. Rust regex and PCRE2 JIT are faster on most text tasks they can run, C Oniguruma wins several individual tasks and compiles some patterns 2x to 4x faster. The highlighting set measured one commit earlier showed a 13 ms regression (C 4.8x faster) on the flat CSS scanner before PR #324 retired the pre-filter there. Upstream Oniguruma ended in April 2025. Supports only ASCII and UTF-8 encodings and not the POSIX/GNU APIs. 8 stars.
corrections.why_faster: Added algorithms, not the language: the matcher keeps C Oniguruma's parser, compiler and VM, but Ferroni adds Rust-only search optimizations (memchr/memmem SIMD scans in place of C's byte loops, literal tries, Aho-Corasick required literals, leading-run skips and jumps, ASCII class runs) and, for TextMate scanning, a regex-automata DFA pre-filter, first-byte dispatch and result/pattern caches (ADR-007, ADR-008).

notes: Real, well-instrumented comparison against C Oniguruma at -O3 with a symmetric harness (both sides go through onig_search with a reused region in benches/general_regex.rs) and every engine validated against Oniguruma's matches; upgraded C to A from in-repo raw data. For wave 14 record same_algorithm false: the 2.2x/1.4x/12x come from Rust-only algorithmic additions (SIMD literal search, tries, Aho-Corasick, run skips, DFA pre-filter from regex-automata), not from Rust codegen, so the entry does not support a language-level claim. Shortcomings: shared virtual CI runners, C wins several tasks and compiles faster, PCRE2 JIT and Rust regex faster on most text tasks.

tier_reason: First-party README tables against GNU sort -u and uniq; the data generator template is in the repo (templates/basic.tera via jen) but no hardware, compiler, coreutils version, locale or timing method is stated, so not A, and no independent measurement exists.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README tables, 25M lines (1.9 GB, 20.67% duplicates), unsorted: runiq -f quick 12.1 s and 298.7 MB vs sort -u 380.2 s and 8.33 GB (about 31x faster, derived from page data); sorted input: runiq -f sorted 10.3 s and 1.3 MB vs uniq 24.9 s and 1.6 MB (about 2.4x, derived). 100M lines (7.7 GB, 55.69% duplicates), unsorted: runiq -f quick 34.7 s vs sort -u 2529.9 s (about 73x, derived); sorted: runiq -f sorted 24.9 s vs uniq 105.8 s (about 4.2x, derived). huniq (Rust) is level with or slightly faster than runiq -f quick (11.9 s and 31.2 s).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the measurements; Cargo.toml release profile now sets lto = true (added 2025-12-13, after the README tables were last changed in January 2024). rustc version, coreutils version and build, and locale not stated.
corrections.caveats: The author says the numbers are a reference for his own tuning, 'not meant to be a competition'; no hardware, compiler, coreutils version, locale or timing tool is given, and the tables date from the January 2024 README updates. The unsorted comparisons are algorithmic (hash set against GNU sort's full external sort, which also produces sorted output rather than first-occurrence order), and GNU sort's speed depends heavily on the locale, which is not stated. The 'quick' filter keeps only xxh64 digests, so a hash collision could drop a unique line (negligible at these sizes but not exact). The sorted-input comparison with uniq is the like-for-like one (src/filters.rs SortedFilter compares each line with the previous one, as uniq does); its 2.4x to 4.2x margin is not explained. huniq, another Rust tool, matches runiq.
corrections.why_faster: README: hash-set ('simple'), pre-hashed xxh64 ('quick') or scalable Bloom filter ('compact') filters instead of sorting the whole input; the 'sorted' filter is the same adjacent-line comparison as uniq, and its margin over GNU uniq is not explained in the README (I/O buffering or locale are possible but unverified).

notes: Numbers match the README exactly. Keep at C: first-party, no hardware or versions, unsorted ratios are hashing against sorting (not a language win); only the sorted runiq-vs-uniq rows compare the same algorithm, and that 2.4x to 4.2x gap is unexplained. same_opt_level unknown (distribution coreutils build not stated).

tier_reason: First-party README output of 'make bench' against cmark; the benchmark code is public (benches/benchmarks.rs, benches/cmark_benchmark.c, Makefile) and the build settings can be read from Cargo.toml and cmark's CMakeLists.txt, but no hardware, compiler versions or cmark commit are given, and the C driver reads an uninitialised accumulator, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README 'make bench' output: rushdown-cached 3.1845 ms, rushdown 3.3427 ms, cmark 3.6439 ms, comrak 4.2451 ms, goldmark 5.6161 ms, pulldown-cmark 6.0037 ms, markdown-rs 89.692 ms. rushdown is about 1.09x faster than cmark when it builds its converter per call as cmark does, and about 1.14x with the converter built once (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust release/bench profile: opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = 'abort' (Cargo.toml). cmark: the master branch zip (unpinned) built with cmark's own Makefile, which passes an empty CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE that cmark's CMakeLists.txt forces to Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG with GCC), as a shared library without LTO; inferred from the build files, no build log. The C timing driver benches/cmark_benchmark.c is compiled with plain gcc and no -O, which only affects the loop around the library call. Compiler versions not stated.
corrections.caveats: Margin is 9% (per-call converter, the like-for-like row) to 14% (cached converter) on a single fixture with no hardware or compiler versions stated, and cmark is downloaded from master at bench time, so its version is unpinned. In benches/cmark_benchmark.c the accumulator 'double sum' is never initialised, so the cmark figure depends on whatever was on the stack (the reported value looks sane, but the harness is undefined behaviour). Different harnesses: Criterion with warm-up for Rust, a 500-iteration gettimeofday loop with no warm-up for cmark. rushdown renders XHTML (xhtml: true) while cmark renders HTML. The Rust harness also runs comrak inside the pulldown-cmark case, inflating that row. Rust side has fat LTO and codegen-units 1, cmark is a non-LTO shared library. No mechanism for the win is given.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated in the README. rushdown is an independent implementation (goldmark-style architecture by goldmark's author) rather than a port of cmark, with an re2rust-generated scanner (Makefile) and memchr for byte search, so any win is from implementation differences, not the language; the 9% margin is within what harness differences (Criterion vs a cold gettimeofday loop, XHTML vs HTML output, LTO) could explain.

notes: Numbers match the README. Keep at C with harness flaws documented: uninitialised 'sum' in the cmark driver (undefined behaviour), unpinned cmark master, asymmetric timing harnesses, no hardware, and only a 9% like-for-like margin on one fixture. Not a language-level win (different implementation); cmark appears to be built Release (-O3) via its CMakeLists default, so no crippled-baseline downgrade.
